item.title: European Ambassador visits Binatang research centre in Madang
item.description: EU Ambassador to PNG, Her Excellency Erika Hasznos paying a courtesy visit to Madang’s Provincial Administrator Daniel Aloi yesterday (Supplied-EU media) The European Ambassador to Papua New Guinea, Her Excellency Erika Hasznos, is impressed with the work of Madang- based Binatang Research Centre.
item.content:encoded:
EU Ambassador to PNG, Her Excellency Erika Hasznos paying a courtesy visit to Madang’s Provincial Administrator Daniel Aloi yesterday (Supplied-EU media)

The European Ambassador to Papua New Guinea, Her Excellency Erika Hasznos, is impressed with the work of Madang- based Binatang Research Centre.

The New Guinea Binatang Research Centre is a biological research and conservation NGO in the country.

Her Excellency Hasznos arrived in Madang yesterday on a two- day visit to the centre where EU is sponsoring 42 students who are currently doing various research works on biodiversity, forestry and climate change.

She said, "The purpose of my visit is to see the project that European Union is funding in Madang. This project is related to forestry, climate change and biodiversity, which is very important here in Papua New Guinea.

"The overall value of this project is more than K220 million, and it focuses on education and young people."

The EU Ambassador took a tour of the research facility at Nagada, outside town, and was impressed with what she saw.

"We would like to empower future environmental leaders of Papua New Guinea because we believe that environmental protection can be built from the bottom. It can be built with young people engaging in education and research, and protecting the environment, the very valuable biodiversity, rainforest, and all the natural aspects, here in Madang and also around Papua New Guinea," she said.

The Madang project focuses on the scholarship of the 42 scholarships for young PNG students who are engaged in Masters studies, in PhD studies and research works.

They are all working in different environmental and biodiversity areas.

"They are also working in partnership with European universities, with researchers from other countries, and together they are making very big contributions to the conservation of the biodiversity of the country," Ambassador Hasznos added.

She was also amazed with the work that the New Guinea Binatang Research Centre is doing in the area of research, conservation and training of young people.

Her Excellency Hasznos said, "I am very impressed with what we've seen so far. We've met alot of scholarship students who are studying under the EU- funding program, we've met several lecturers, researches, and they have also shown us how the Binatang Research Centre is connected to this project, and what it is doing to preserving and also researching the biodiversity of Papua New Guinea.

"We've also seen an enormous amount of species that the centre has already categorised, and how this these educational networks are building students from Madang, Papua New Guinea and also from Europe," the EU Ambassador stated.

Her Excellency Hasznos is also the Head of the European Union delegation to Papua New Guinea.

Today, she will be witnessing the graduation of 21 scholars who have attended a biological course.

The scholars were also taken on field trips and training in the night at Wanang Swire Conservation Station.

They also went for an Ecological field trip to Manam Island last week.

item.title: Kagamuga runway nears completion and reopening
item.description: The runway maintenance at the Mt Hagen Kagamuga Airport is nearing completion with 510 meters yet to be upgraded to fully complete the rehabilitation program currently underway (Supplied) Highlands’s travellers are looking forward to the full reopening of the Mt Hagen's Kagamuga Airport runway, with rehabilitation work now reaching about 76 percent of its full length.
item.content:encoded:
The runway maintenance at the Mt Hagen Kagamuga Airport is nearing completion with 510 meters yet to be upgraded to fully complete the rehabilitation program currently underway (Supplied)

Highlands’s travellers are looking forward to the full reopening of the Mt Hagen's Kagamuga Airport runway, with rehabilitation work now reaching about 76 percent of its full length.

The National Airports Corporation (NAC) says the runway rehabilitation is progressing steadily, with 1,680 metres now available for aircraft operations.

In a press statement issued earlier this week (171126), the NAC states this is an increase from the 1,190 metres available in October 2026.

The extension is already allowing larger aircraft such as the Fokker 70 and ATR 72 to operate at the airport.

But there are still 510 metres of runway to be rehabilitated before the full length can be restored.

It stresses that if the weather permits, the work is expected to be completed ahead of the peak travel period (which is around November-February).

The update is being closely watched by travelers, businesses, and communities up in the Highlands, who have been waiting for Kagamuga Airport to return to full capacity.

The airport is an important link for people traveling in and out of Western Highlands and the entire Highlands region, particularly for passengers and businesses relying on air transport.

The NAC further states that it is working with contractors and aviation stakeholders to complete the project safely, efficiently, and with minimal disruption to airport operations.

Once the rehabilitation is completed, the restored runway will allow larger aircraft, including Boeing 737 and Airbus A220 aircraft, to operate at Mt Hagen Kagamuga Airport.

The NAC says this will improve passenger and freight access, strengthen regional air connectivity, and support economic activity in the Highlands.

For travellers, however, the focus is now on seeing the remaining 510 metres completed and the runway fully restored.

The NAC has thanked airlines, passengers and communities in WHP, Highlands and PNG as a whole for their patience and understanding as the rehabilitation work continues.

item.title: Families pay thousands as PNG wait for specialist doctors
item.description: Dr. Mitchell Masin (right) who is another of the two plastic surgeons in PNG during an operation of a cleft lip child patient at the Mt Hagen Provincial Specialist Hospital last week (Supplied) Families in Papua New Guinea are waiting months and sometimes years for specialised medical services, with some spending thousands of kina travelling long distances just to give their loved ones a chance at
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Mitchell Masin (right) who is another of the two plastic surgeons in PNG during an operation of a cleft lip child patient at the Mt Hagen Provincial Specialist Hospital last week (Supplied)

Families in Papua New Guinea are waiting months and sometimes years for specialised medical services, with some spending thousands of kina travelling long distances just to give their loved ones a chance at a normal life.

The shortage of specialist doctors, including plastic surgeons, means life-changing surgery is often only available when specialist teams travel to the provinces.

This was the case in Mt Hagen last week, where more than 20 children were given a new chance to speak, eat and smile after undergoing surgery for cleft lip and cleft palate.

The children were among 28 patients treated by an Interplast surgical team from Port Moresby General Hospital during a four-day visit to the Mt Hagen Provincial Specialist Hospital.

The youngest patient was only five months old.

The visiting team included PNG's only two plastic surgeons, Dr Jackson Nuli (Team Leader/surgeon) and Dr Mitchell Masin (surgeon), and anaesthetist Dr. Hilbert Tovirika.

Dr Nuli says the demand for plastic surgery in PNG is high, particularly among children born with cleft lip and cleft palate.

"For our country the big need is children with cleft lip and palate; those are the ones that we need to get them at their early age and operate on at least by one to complete lip and palate surgery.

"But most of the children they come late like one or two years late which is one of our challenges and the reason is because we don't have enough plastic surgeons throughout the country which is also the reason why we are moving right throughout PNG as there's need everywhere and until and unless we have enough plastic surgeons in the country, we should be ok."

Dr Nuli also says the country does not have enough plastic surgeons to provide specialised services in all hospitals.

Because of the shortage, the Interplast team travels to provincial hospitals and health authorities where patients have already been screened and where funding and other support are available.

For families in remote and rural communities, however, accessing specialist care can come at a heavy cost.

Some have to travel to major centres, pay for transport and accommodation, and wait for long periods before a specialist service becomes available.

For children born with cleft lip or cleft palate, that wait can affect their ability to eat and speak and can continue to affect them as they grow.

For some of the children treated in Mt Hagen, this was their first opportunity to have the condition corrected.

The Inter-Plast team leader Dr Nuli adds Mt Hagen is the second hospital the team has visited this year, after Buka.

The team will next travel to Kimbe to provide surgery for children with cleft lip and palate, as well as adults with burns, wounds and other physical deformities.

Several adults in Mt Hagen were also treated for old burns and wounds that had caused parts of their skin to become attached.

Anaesthetist Dr Hilbert Tovirika says his role is to keep patients safely under anaesthesia while surgeons carry out the operations.

He stresses that the team faces challenges during surgery and depends on the quick response of local health authorities when equipment or other support is urgently needed.

"Challenges we face across the country during the operations are things like consumables, machines, sometimes we fall short of things needed in the operating room, blood results, and tests that we require. Like Mt Hagen Hospital was short of things to do blood test and when we arrived, thanks to the hospital management managed to bring in things needed quickly so that we can be able to check the patients' blood level before they go in for operation just to make sure everything is safe."

" Otherwise if problems are encountered along the way, patients can die which are the real happenings."

This is the second time the Inter-Plast team has carried out plastic surgery in Mt Hagen.

Last year (2025), the team also treated 28 patients, mostly children, during a four-day visit.

The repeated visits highlight a bigger problem for PNG's public health system-the growing demand for specialist services and the limited number of specialist doctors available to provide them.

Local medical estimates reported that between 100 and 200 babies are born with cleft deformities in PNG every year.

With the number of patients requiring specialised treatment increasing, the two plastic surgeons currently available in the country cannot meet the demand alone.

The Inter-Plast outreach programme is therefore helping take specialised surgery closer to patients who would otherwise have to travel to Port Moresby or wait even longer for treatment.

But the visits also raise a bigger question for PNG's health system-how long can patients continue to wait for specialist services to come to them?

item.title: Mian tribe in Gumine district of Simbu received relief food supplies

The relief was for families hit hard by the El Niño drought (Supplied) "People who owe you nothing chose to give back from their own hard work because they feel a sense of belonging. What you are receiving today is the direct result of educati
item.content:encoded:
Hundreds of Mian villagers gather as 800 bags of Roots Rice, cooking oil and salt worth over K60,000 are laid out for distribution by the Mian Elites Union. The relief was for families hit hard by the El Niño drought (Supplied)

"People who owe you nothing chose to give back from their own hard work because they feel a sense of belonging. What you are receiving today is the direct result of education.

The next time you are selling goods by the roadside and see a student walking to school, share what you have with them because tomorrow, they will be the ones returning to lift up this community."

Those were the words of community leader Ian Gore, as more than 4,000 residents of the Mian Tribe in Gumine District of Simbu received critical food relief following a major fundraising drive by the Mian Elites Union (MEU), a network of Mian professionals and working-class members based across Papua New Guinea and abroad.

The relief effort, which raised over K60,000, was delivered recently providing an unprecedented lifeline to communities severely impacted by the ongoing El Niño drought.

Local villagers described the aid as both historic and timely, observing that prolonged dry weather had completely destroyed their subsistence food gardens. Many families had been forced to exhaust personal savings earmarked for other essential needs just to survive day-to-day prior to the union's intervention.

Funds raised by the union including international contributions from supporters in China and the Canberra Adventist Church in Australia were used to procure bulk staple supplies, alongside covering vehicle hire and fuel logistics.

The distributed relief package included 800 bags of 10kg Roots Rice, 100 boxes of 1 litre cooking oil and 50 bales of 500g salt.

Supplies were allocated across local wards using verified household registries, ensuring each family received a 10kg bag of rice, one litre of cooking oil, and a packet of salt.

Emmanuel Kumulgo, Chairman of MEU, extended his official gratitude to the sons, daughters, and extended families of the greater Mian Tribe in Gumine District for mobilizing to support their kin.

"While a 10kg bag of rice, cooking oil, and salt may not sustain a household through to the end of the year, our hope is that it eases your immediate burden while you find alternative ways to get by," Mr Kumulgo said.

He also stressed that the initiative was strictly humanitarian and free of political agendas, urging community members not to spread misinformation that could sow division. Instead, he noted, the relief drive sets a precedent for tribal unity in the face of future natural disasters.

Echoing the theme of community responsibility, Gore urged residents to champion education as the ultimate catalyst for change.

item.title: Police seize 196 cartons of beer at Maip check point in Enga
item.description: Police have intercepted and seized 196 cartons of SP Beer at the Maip Police Check Point during an extension of drunk patrol operations to Porgera in Enga Province. Enga Provincial Police Commander, Acting Superintendent Daniel Yangen, confirmed the seizure on November 12, saying police intercepted a truck allegedly transporting the alcohol into Porgera.
item.content:encoded:
Police have intercepted and seized 196 cartons of SP Beer at the Maip Police Check Point during an extension of drunk patrol operations to Porgera in Enga Province.

Enga Provincial Police Commander, Acting Superintendent Daniel Yangen, confirmed the seizure on November 12, saying police intercepted a truck allegedly transporting the alcohol into Porgera.

According to a media release from the Provincial Police Commander's Office, police believe the truck was travelling via the Mendi–Kandep route in an attempt to avoid detection and bypass checkpoints at Wabag and Laiagam.

PPC Yangen said the interception resulted from the extension of drunk patrols and law-and-order operations from Wabag to Laiagam and further into Porgera.

"This is a major success for our operation. The smuggling of large quantities of alcohol into Porgera is fuelling drunk and disorderly behaviour, tribal fights, traffic accidents and other crimes. We will not allow it to continue," PPC Yangen said.

The truck, driver and crew have reportedly been detained for questioning, while the seized beer has been secured at the Pogera police station as exhibits pending further investigations and possible charges under the Liquor Act.

PPC Yangen commended officers at the Maip Police Check Point for their vigilance and professionalism, warning that police would intensify checkpoints and patrols along entry routes into Enga, including the Mendi–Kandep route, during the festive season.

He also called on the public to report suspected alcohol smuggling to police.

item.title: Schouten Island communities call for urgent El Nino assistance
item.description: Photo showing garden food on Ruprup Island affected by prolonged El-Nino heat affecting livelihood of Schouten Islands Communities (Supplied) Communities from the Schouten Islands in East Sepik are calling for urgent government assistance as they face severe food and water shortages caused by the El Nino weather conditions.
item.content:encoded:
Photo showing garden food on Ruprup Island affected by prolonged El-Nino heat affecting livelihood of Schouten Islands Communities (Supplied)

Communities from the Schouten Islands in East Sepik are calling for urgent government assistance as they face severe food and water shortages caused by the El Nino weather conditions.

Pastor Adrian Reim of Ruprup Island told NBC News that communities have been affected since June 2026 but have not received assistance from the National Government's El Nino relief funds.

He said only Biem Island had received two food relief deliveries from Wewak district, one in August and another in October, while other island communities were still waiting for assistance.

Pastor Reim said bananas, their main staple food usually eaten with fish, had dried up because of the prolonged dry conditions.

"Our staple food is banana to go with fish. Currently, the bananas have dried and we are living on breadfruit, locally known as kapiak, and mango," he said.

Biem Island community leader and spokesperson John Wange said the situation had become increasingly difficult, with the limited food relief lasting only one or two meals.

"We don't have any more hope. Little food relief from Wewak District is for one or two meals only," Mr Wange said

He also raised concerns over the island's water shortage, saying residents were now travelling by dinghy to Ruprup Island, about an hour away, to collect water.

"Currently, Biem Island has no water at all, so we have to use a boat to Ruprup Island, about an hour by dinghy, to fetch water," he said.

Despite this, Caretaker Provincial Administrator Alphonse Kami told NBC News that all six districts in East Sepik, as well as the Provincial Government, had received their K2.5 million, fifty percent of the El Nino funding allocation.

Mr Kami called on the districts to follow the required administrative processes to access and use the funds. He said District Administrators chair their respective District El Nino Committees and are responsible for developing plans to deliver assistance, while the Provincial Administration provides oversight.

However, NBC News understands that districts are yet to delivered relief supplies to affected communities using the K2.5 million El Nino funding allocation from the National Government.

item.title: Governor Pariwa warns finance officers against 10 per cent cuts
item.description: Governor Ramsey Pariwa welcoming Madang’s new PFM, Lovelyn Gordon (NBC News) Madang Governor, Ramsey Pariwa, has issued a stern warning to officers working in the Madang Provincial Finance Office (PFO) and District Finance Offices (DFO) in the province against getting 10 per cent cuts for services rendered to clients.
item.content:encoded:
Governor Ramsey Pariwa welcoming Madang’s new PFM, Lovelyn Gordon (NBC News)

Madang Governor, Ramsey Pariwa, has issued a stern warning to officers working in the Madang Provincial Finance Office (PFO) and District Finance Offices (DFO) in the province against getting 10 per cent cuts for services rendered to clients.

Governor Pariwa issued the warning recently when farewelling the outgoing Provincial Finance Manager for Madang George Memke, and welcoming the incoming PFM, Lovelyn Gordon.

Governor Pariwa reminded the finance officers from all the six districts of Madang who gathered for the HOTO ceremony that as public servants, their responsibility is to serve.

Mr. Pariwa stated that from his experience in the last four years he had come to realize how important the job of the PFM is, therefore, he made it his personal business to attend the HOTO ceremony to bid farewell to his hard-working friend and outgoing PFM George Memke, and wish him well in the next career he is pursuing.

He said that the little 10 per cent cuts that certain Finance officers receive or intentional delay in processing of cheques or financial documentation must cease and processes improved forthwith.

Mr. Pariwa said there have been grievances raised before him by District MPs and LLG presidents regarding the performances of DFM and DFOs.

“Let me be frank that the LLG presidents in Bogia are not receiving funds since July because the DFO is not in order,” Mr. Pariwa stated.

The governor was in Bogia in Almami LLG in August to attend to some important programs to support the thirty-six (36) wards, but there was no funding made available to support these wards.

Apparently, these wards were supposed to receive K1,000 each to open ward accounts at the bank. To this date, that has not happened.

“I will be happy to refer people, for and on behalf of the best interest of my people, to make sure you are held accountable.

“I know, and I won’t call names. It's not good. Madang is a small place,” Mr Pariwa stressed.

Governor Pariwa highlighted that a similar Ward program was staged in Usino LLG at the end of last month and the program turned out remarkably well.

“If Usino LLG can run claims, print cheques, and release funds for its respective wards, then why not Bogia?” Mr. Pariwa questioned.

He told the officers from the Madang PFO and the six DFOs that he usually copes the blame for the officers’ mishap.

“The people don’t blame you. They blame me. They don’t know what you do and don’t know your name as well as the position you occupy.

“They are ordinary people and their minds are straightforward. It is yes or no, so to speak,” Mr Pariwa added.

Governor Pariwa encouraged the Finance officers from the PFO and the DFO to change and improve their attitude during the transition with the new PFM coming in to polish up on their performances.

“I am happy to work with you and support you for a better outcome,” Governor Pariwa affirmed.

item.title: Rise in fuel price hits Lae transport operators
item.description: The higher fares are making it harder for some passengers to afford taxi services, while drivers are also seeing fewer customers (NBC News) Taxi and PMV operators in Lae say the increase in fuel prices, with petrol rising to K7 per litre, is cutting into their daily earnings and making it harder to keep their vehicles on the road.
item.content:encoded:
The higher fares are making it harder for some passengers to afford taxi services, while drivers are also seeing fewer customers (NBC News)

Taxi and PMV operators in Lae say the increase in fuel prices, with petrol rising to K7 per litre, is cutting into their daily earnings and making it harder to keep their vehicles on the road.

Taxi operator Nickson Kongdorap, from Western Highlands Province, says before the increase, his daily takings were between K250 and K300, with about K100 spent on fuel.

He says his daily takings have now dropped to around K200, but he still spends about K100 on fuel, leaving him with less money for other expenses.

Another taxi operator, Malakai Kisbar, also from Western Highlands, says he has increased his fares to meet the rising costs.

Kisbar says short taxi trips that previously cost K10 are now charged at K20.

He says the higher fares are making it harder for some passengers to afford taxi services, while drivers are also seeing fewer customers.

PMV operators are also dealing with higher fuel costs.

A PMV driver who spoke on Friday says K50 previously bought about 10 litres of fuel, but now buys only around six litres.

The rising costs are affecting both transport operators and passengers, with drivers struggling to maintain their earnings while customers face higher transport expenses.
